analysis.one_liner: Requires construction employers to give workers one paid 15-minute break every four hours.
analysis.headline: The bill would have given construction workers a paid 15-minute break for every four hours worked, but it never received a committee hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 785 would have amended federal labor law to require construction employers to give workers a paid 15-minute rest break for every four hours of work [S2][S3]. Employers would have to tell new hires about this right in their primary language, post signs about it in English and Spanish at work sites, and could not retaliate against workers who take breaks or complain to the Department of Labor [S2][S3]. The bill died after being referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which never acted on it before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Construction workers — including those hired as contractors — who would get a guaranteed paid 15-minute break for every four hours worked, notice of that right at hiring in their own language, and protection from being fired or punished for taking breaks or filing complaints [S2][S3]. Construction is physically demanding and often outdoors, so scheduled breaks matter for fatigue and heat safety. The bill's protections floor at existing law: it would not override any state law, local ordinance, or union contract requiring longer breaks [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Guarantees construction employees at least one 15-minute paid rest break for every four hours of work, a right federal law does not currently provide, since federal law requires pay for short breaks but does not require employers to offer them.

Requires employers to notify new hires of their break rights in the employee's primary language and to post signs in both English and Spanish at work sites — meaningful in an industry where many workers are Spanish-speaking.
Prohibits retaliation against workers who request breaks or file a complaint with the Labor Department, with remedies including reinstatement, back pay, and equal liquidated damages.
Lets the Labor Department assess an administrative penalty against an employer who fails to fix a violation within 30 days of notice.

analysis.who_pays: Construction employers, who would give up roughly 15 minutes of productive time per worker per four hours (about 6% of paid time) and would bear the cost of that paid time, plus compliance costs for hiring notices and required signage [S2][S3]. Consumers could see some of that cost passed through in construction prices.

drawbacks.text: Paid breaks are a real cost to employers — about 6% of paid work time per covered worker — which falls hardest on small contractors operating on thin margins, and some of it would likely be passed to customers in bids and prices.

The bill covers only construction employees; it offers nothing to workers in other physically demanding industries such as warehousing, agriculture, or manufacturing, who get no rest-break right from it.

Employers already must pay workers for short breaks under existing federal law, so the bill's net effect on pay is limited; its main change is requiring that the breaks actually be offered and adding paperwork and enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker benefit is real but modest and well-targeted: a guaranteed paid break plus anti-retaliation protection in one of the country's most physically dangerous industries, at a cost of about 6% of paid time to employers. The design is reasonable — it respects stronger state laws and union contracts and adds enforcement teeth — though its narrow scope leaves comparable workers in other industries uncovered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sylvia Garcia of Texas introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, with 13 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, the committee with jurisdiction over federal labor law.

That was the last action ever taken on the bill. The committee held no markup, reported nothing, and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, at which point the bill died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction employers come out ahead: they avoid the cost and compliance burden of mandatory paid rest breaks and federal anti-retaliation enforcement, without any vote ever being taken on the merits.

for.name: Rep. Sylvia Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a federal paid rest-break requirement for construction workers.

for.name: 13 House Democrats, including Reps. Katie Porter, Judy Chu, Betty McCollum, Greg Casar, and Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the bill; all 13 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — over the remaining two years of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House floor agenda and never scheduled the bill for a vote, though no vote was ever requested because the bill never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it died in a committee controlled by the Republican House majority without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have cost construction employers roughly 15 paid minutes per worker per four hours, plus notice and signage duties and exposure to Labor Department penalties for retaliation. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against workers' interest in guaranteed breaks.

Because the bill defines a construction employee to include workers hired as contractors of an employer, staffing firms and subcontractors that supply construction labor would have been covered by the same break, notice, and anti-retaliation requirements.
